name: Adal Sultanate and Aussa
summary: A Muslim sultanate in the Horn of Africa whose leader Ahmad ibn Ibrahim (Gragn) nearly conquered Ethiopia (1529–43); after its fall its heirs ruled the Afar region of Aussa.

location.value: Horn of Africa. The capital was Dakkar (1415–1520), then Harar (1520–1577); Zeila was a major port.

terrain.value: Highlands, semi-desert plains and a hot coast on the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

climate.value: Hot and dry, with little rain.

resources.value: Livestock, salt, ivory and trade goods.

population.value: The article gives no population total.

urbanisation.value: Mostly villages; a royal capital and market towns.

disease.value: Malaria and other tropical diseases; smallpox outbreaks.

migration.value: Oromo migrations in the 1500s weakened Adal and reshaped the region.

economicBase.value: Trade in gold, ivory and slaves (slaves were shipped from Zeila to Persia, Arabia, Egypt and India), plus millet, cattle, barley and khat for Yemen. The page does not name herding as a main base.

tradeRoutes.value: The ports of Zeila and Berbera carried goods to Arabia, India and Egypt.

wealth.value: Trade wealth came from slaves, ivory, coffee and livestock.

moneyAndTax.value: The ashrafi is listed as the currency; merchants used imported Egyptian dinars and dirhams. The article does not mention cowrie shells.

inequality.value: Rulers and nobles above free farmers; enslaved people at the bottom.

governmentType.value: Sultanate (Walashma dynasty); after 1577 the capital moved to Aussa and the state became the Imamate of Aussa.

keyRulers.value: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim, called “Imam” in the article; “Gragn” appears only in local tradition.

succession.value: The Walashma dynasty ruled at first, followed by military imams.

institutions.value: Islamic courts and a sultan advised by religious scholars.

stability.value: Long wars with Christian Ethiopia kept the region unstable.

eliteConflict.value: Sultans and military leaders such as Ahmad ibn Ibrahim (Gragn) competed for power.

armyAndTech.value: Ottoman musketeers were requested by the Imam after Portuguese defeats; the article gives no date.

territoryChange.value: Held a territory from Zeila to Massawa and some inland Abyssinian areas; invaded Tigray in 1535.

alliancesRivals.value: Ottomans helped Adal against Ethiopia, while Portugal helped Ethiopia.

scienceEducation.value: Oral learning; Qur’anic schools where Islam spread.

openness.value: Open to Muslim trade networks across the Red Sea.

communicationTransport.value: Camel caravans and coastal ships carried goods.

religion.value: Sunni Islam (Shafi'i school), with Sufi groups such as the Ba 'Alawiyya and Shadhili.

languageWriting.value: Harari, Somali and Afar were spoken, with Arabic used for writing.

artsArchitecture.value: The city walls of Harar, built by Nur ibn Mujahid.

sharedIdentity.value: A shared Muslim identity opposed to the Christian highland state.

dailyLife.value: Pastoral families herded camels and cattle, while townspeople traded and farmed.

neighbours.value: The Ethiopian Empire to the west and the Ottomans across the Red Sea.

ideasReligions.value: Islamic scholarship and Sufi brotherhoods shaped the sultanate.

colonisation.value: Aussa absorbed into Italian East Africa (1936).

riseSignals.value: Founded by Sabr ad-Din III on the Harar plateau (infobox date 1415).

peakPeriod.value: Disputed. The page links the height to Imam Ahmad's conquest of Abyssinia (war 1529–43), but also says the state reached its height under Sultan Badlay and, elsewhere, that Adal 'attained its peak in the 14th century'.

declineSignals.value: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim (Gragn) was killed in 1543, ending the great Adal conquests.

outcome.value: Disestablished in 1577; Muhammad Gasa founded the Imamate of Aussa.

overallCertainty.value: Known from oral traditions, travellers and colonial records; many dates are approximate.
